en-01-tip.caption:
Nobody opens a business with a system. They open it with a notebook, a bank app and a drawer, and the system is supposed to arrive later. Often it does not.

The people who get there did not buy software or go on a course. They made one small decision and then kept making it. The next thing that happens gets written down. The invoice goes in the same place every time. The receipt gets photographed on the day, not in April. The mileage goes in the same note it went in last week.

That is the whole of it. A system is not a thing you install, it is one habit repeated until it looks organised from the outside.

And if this year has got away from you, that is not a character flaw. It is a Thursday. Start with the next thing.
en-01-tip.ask: Save this for the week that gets away from you.
en-01-tip.title: A system is one small decision, repeated

en-02-acq.caption:
The first half hour with us costs nothing. Not a reduced rate, not an introductory offer. Free, thirty minutes, and no bill at the end of it.

That is deliberate. People were putting off the conversation because they assumed an invoice came with it, and then a year went past, and the thing they were worried about got bigger rather than smaller.

Here is what actually happens in that half hour. You tell us what the business is, what you are filing at the moment, and the parts you are not sure about. We tell you what needs doing, and what it would cost if you wanted us to do it. If the answer is that you are fine as you are, we say that too.

Thirty minutes is enough to get the shape of it. That is the only thing it is for.
en-02-acq.ask: Share this with someone who keeps putting the conversation off.
en-02-acq.title: The first thirty minutes with us are free

en-03-acq.caption:
A lot of people believe they are stuck where they are until the year end. You are not. A limited company can change accountant mid-year, and it happens every week of the year.

There is no rule that ties a move to an accounting date. You pick a date, we take the filings on from it, and you carry on trading through all of it. Nothing has to stop and nothing has to wait for March.

The one honest thing to say is that waiting rarely improves it. If something is not right now, it will not be more right in eight months, and the records only drift further from the person who made them.

If you have already been thinking about it, that is usually your answer.
en-03-acq.ask: Save this for the day you decide you have waited long enough.
en-03-acq.title: You can change accountant mid-year, not just at year end

en-04-acq.caption:
You do not have to be near us to be with us. Everything we do runs by phone and by message, and our clients are spread right across the UK.

What that looks like in practice: you photograph an invoice between jobs and send it straight over. Sign-up happens remotely. Records come in however you already keep them, not in some format you have to learn. Questions get answered in a message instead of a meeting you had to take an afternoon off for.

There are two offices if you ever want to sit across a desk from someone, and some people do that once, at the start. Most never need to.

Same accountant, same filings, same dates watched for you. Just none of the travelling.
en-04-acq.ask: Share this with someone who thinks they are too far away.
en-04-acq.title: All of it online, wherever you are in the UK

en-05-edu.caption:
Add up everything you sold over the last twelve months. Not the tax year, not your accounting year: any twelve months in a row, looked at again as each month ends. If that total goes over £90,000, you have to register for VAT.

Two things people get wrong. It is what you sold, not what you kept, so it is sales before costs and not profit. And because it rolls, a quiet spring does not cancel out a busy autumn.

There is a second test that catches people. If you expect to go over £90,000 in the next 30 days on its own, and one large contract can do that, you register straight away.

Once you have crossed the line, you have 30 days from the end of the month you crossed in to register with HMRC.

It works downwards too. If your sales fall below £88,000 you can ask HMRC to cancel the registration.

Who this does not touch: businesses selling only things that are VAT exempt or outside the scope of VAT, whatever their size. If you are at £90,000 or below you can still register by choice, and a business whose sales are wholly or mainly zero-rated can apply to be exempt from registering.
en-05-edu.ask: Save this one — the £90,000 and £88,000 figures are worth having to hand.
en-05-edu.title: Add up what you sold — the VAT line is £90,000

en-06-edu.caption:
Registering the company at Companies House told HMRC nothing. Two bodies, two registers, two sets of forms, and that gap is where most of the first-year trouble starts.

Once the company is active, you have 3 months from the start of its tax accounting period to tell HMRC. You do that online through the company's business tax account, with the date activity started, the company's registered details and the accounting reference date.

Active is wider than people expect. It is not only selling things. Carrying on a trade or a profession counts, and so does any other income, which includes interest earned on the company bank account. Writing a business plan or choosing a name does not by itself make the company active.

The usual way people discover they missed it is a notice to deliver a return arriving a couple of years later.

Now the dormant position, because that is the common misunderstanding. A company HMRC accepts as dormant does not have to file a Company Tax Return, but only once the company has actually told HMRC and HMRC has confirmed it. A company that simply stops trading and says nothing is still required to submit a Corporation Tax return. And being dormant for Corporation Tax changes nothing at Companies House: dormant accounts and a confirmation statement are still due.

If you are not certain which of the two you have spoken to, that is a short check and a much better afternoon than the one the notice gives you.
en-06-edu.ask: Save this if you have set a company up in the last year.
en-06-edu.title: You have 3 months to tell HMRC the company started trading

en-07-edu.caption:
Black Friday is tomorrow and invoices will be flying. Worth knowing which ones count.

Sell to another VAT-registered person and you must give them a VAT invoice: it is their evidence for reclaiming the VAT. A full one shows 11 items — a sequential number uniquely identifying the document; the time of supply, which is the tax point; the date of issue where that differs; your name, address and VAT registration number; the customer's name and address; a description identifying the goods or services; for each description the quantity, the VAT rate and the amount payable excluding VAT; the gross total excluding VAT; the rate of any cash discount offered; the total VAT chargeable; and the unit price. The total VAT must be in sterling even where the rest of the invoice is in another currency.

For a supply of £250 or less you can issue a simplified VAT invoice instead, if your customer agrees. That needs 4 items: your name, address and VAT number; the tax point; a description; and, for each VAT rate, the total payable including VAT and the rate. For more than £250 it has to be the full invoice, and you must issue a full one at any value if the customer asks.

You normally have 30 days from the tax point to issue it.

Where it does not apply: zero-rated supplies need no VAT invoice, and nor does a customer who is not VAT registered. A simplified one is out if the customer does not agree, above £250, or, in Northern Ireland, for a customer in an EU member state.
en-07-edu.ask: Save this before the weekend's invoices start going out.
en-07-edu.title: Up to £250 a shorter VAT invoice will do — above it, all 11 items

en-08-joke.caption:
It lands in every accountant's phone eventually. A photograph, no message, and then the question.

The answer turns on facts, not on how the question is put. What does the business actually use it for, how much of the time, and could you show that to someone who asked? Something the business genuinely needs is usually fine. Something bought for the house, with a reason found for it afterwards, stays a personal purchase however it is described.

This week that matters more than usual. Black Friday puts a lot of large one-off purchases on business cards in a single weekend, and by February nobody can remember which were which. A note on the day, saying what the thing is for and who uses it, is most of the job.
en-08-joke.ask: Share this with the one person you know who would ask it.
en-08-joke.title: The question every accountant gets at eleven at night

en-09-joke.caption:
Every accountant has had this client, and honestly he is one of the good ones. He did the thing we ask for. Photograph the receipt on the day, while you still know what it was for. Twelve months of it, without being chased once.

Then you open the folder. Half of them are a thumb. A few are a tablecloth. Several are beautifully sharp pictures of the top of a receipt, where the shop logo is, and not the part with the date and the total on it.

A photo counts as a record if it can be read. Supplier, date, total, and the VAT where there is any. That is all it has to show, and the paper original can go in the bin once it does.

The fix takes about ten seconds and you only do it once. Take the first photo, actually look at it, and if the date and the total are there, carry on exactly as you have been for the rest of the year.
en-09-joke.ask: Share this with whoever photographs their receipts one-handed.
en-09-joke.title: A year of receipt photos, all of them thumb

en-10-quote.caption:
It was a private notebook, never meant for readers. The line sits in the seventh part of what we now call the Meditations, and the frame carries a shortened version of it — his own words, kept short enough to fit, and stopping at the end of the thought. In full it runs: “Never let the future disturb you. You will meet it, if you have to, with the same weapons of reason which today arm you against the present.”

It is a useful thing to read in late November, when next year starts arriving in the post. The January filing. The VAT return. December payroll, early. The quiet trading weeks after Christmas. None of it is here yet.

And his point is not that it will be easy. It is that you will not be a worse version of yourself when it comes. The same head that is reading this is the one that will deal with it.

What you can do tonight is not worry better. It is get the thing out of your head and onto a list, so the future has somewhere to sit until it is due.
en-10-quote.ask: Save this one for a week in January.
en-10-quote.title: Never let the future disturb you
